summary:
Ekaterina Deyneka opens by polling the room: nearly everyone has recorded video at conferences, almost no one posts it; she counts herself in that gap. Reelful is her answer—an agentic video editor aimed at the mass consumer rather than professional editors. The user drops in raw media (photos and video) plus a direction such as 'add captions, add music, add voiceover,' and the agent handles the rest: understanding the media, transcribing speech, selecting the strongest moments, omitting bad takes and pauses, and producing a ready-to-share clip complete with captions, music, voiceover, B-roll, and animated stills.

Framed for an AI engineering audience, Deyneka argues an agentic video editor is structurally the same shape as an agentic app builder: prompt goes in, a remote sandbox spins up, an agent works inside it with tools and skills, and a finished artifact renders out the other end (an app preview versus a rendered video). The key difference is editing versus generating. A blank canvas lets an agent do whatever it wants; real footage forces the agent to judge which take is best, what to drop, and how to make messy or incomplete material look polished.

The Reelful pipeline begins with media understanding and transcription, then produces a creative plan the user can approve before editing begins. Inside the sandbox, the agent carries 'skills'—cut rules, font pairings, B-roll conventions, taste and craft—where the house style lives. Composition is done in Remotion, an open-source framework that expresses video as React code, chosen because agents write code well. A verification layer checks the composition will render and sends the agent back to iterate if it won't. To reach consumers, Reelful hides this complexity behind mobile-first directional templates and a familiar building-style editor for final tweaks. The speaker demoed examples assembled entirely by the agent and announced Reelful is funded by a16z speedrun.

sections.title: The problem: recording vs. posting video
sections.summary: Deyneka polls the room: nearly everyone has recorded video at conferences, almost no one posts it. She admits she is in that gap—records a lot but never posts because video editing is hard, tedious, and largely manual. This is the motivation for Reelful.

sections.title: What agentic video editing is
sections.summary: User drops in media (photos and videos) plus context or directions (captions, music, voiceover). The agent understands the media, finds the right moments, assembles them, and generates captions, music, voiceover, and B-rolls into a ready-to-share clip. Example: removing pauses and unsuccessful takes from a speak-to-camera recording.

sections.title: Structural parallel to an agentic app builder
sections.summary: For an AI engineering audience: agentic video editor and agentic app builder share the same shape—prompt in (media + prompt vs. prompt), remote sandbox spins up, agent with tools/skills works inside, output renders (rendered video vs. app preview).

sections.title: Editing is harder than generating
sections.summary: Reelful focuses on editing real footage rather than generating from scratch. A blank canvas lets an agent do anything; real footage forces it to judge the best take, decide what to omit, and still deliver a polished result from messy or incomplete material so viewers cannot tell if it was AI- or human-edited.

sections.title: The Reelful pipeline
sections.summary: Step-by-step walkthrough: media understanding + speech transcription → creative plan for user approval → sandbox spins up with agent carrying skills (cut rules, font pairings, B-roll taste/craft) → agent can spawn sub-processes for music, voiceover, sounds, photo animation → Remotion composition expressed as React code (chosen because agents write code well) → verification layer checks the composition will render and iterates if not.

sections.title: Hiding the pipeline from mass consumers
sections.summary: The complex workflow is deliberately hidden. Reelful goes mobile-first so users can edit while driving, walking, or lifting. To address prompting difficulty, they ship directional templates (speak-to-camera, add B-rolls, voiceover) that work with just dropped media. A familiar building-style editor is added so users can tweak agent-generated clips (e.g., trim a second or correct a caption word).

sections.title: Demo and announcement
sections.summary: Speaker plays a demo clip about a 'creators dinner' event and notes all demo clips were agent-assembled with no traditional editor and already posted on social media. She announces Reelful's second version is available for attendees to try and that the company was recently funded by a16z speedrun.

sections.title: Closing
sections.summary: Speaker asks the audience to film a brief video together as a meta nod to the talk's topic.

demonstrations: A polished clip about a 'creators dinner' event (lobster, blue crab, private chefs from LA, tropical sunset venue, gifts) was played; speaker stated all such demo clips were assembled using only the agent, no regular video editor, and were already posted on social media.
Speaker shows an agentic pipeline diagram with two parallel columns (agentic app builder vs. agentic video editor) sharing the same prompt → sandbox → agent → output shape.
limitations: Agent can make mistakes writing the Remotion composition; the verification layer exists specifically to catch this and trigger iteration.
Real footage can be messy or incomplete, yet the agent is expected to still deliver a polished, professionally made result indistinguishable from human-edited.
Prompting videos can be challenging for users, which is why Reelful ships preset directional templates (speak-to-camera, add B-rolls, voiceover) so users can edit without writing any prompt.
Agentic video editing is described as a 'complex workflow' that ideally consumers should never even know about.
